taxonomy.note: Accepted by current Kew/POWO; native from Oklahoma through Texas into northeastern and central Mexico.

evidence: Hays — UT Plant Resources Center Purola Preserve documents M. reverchonii in the natural flora.
Williamson — UT Plant Resources Center provides a detailed field treatment.
Travis — USDA ARS herbarium specimen NA0074024 was collected along upper Bull Creek, about 7 mi NW of Austin.
target_zone_range.guardrail: Use exact specimen/local-flora evidence; do not infer counties solely from Edwards Plateau or Blackland Prairie ecoregion presence.

morphology.look_here_first: Start with plant size and blade texture. Seep muhly is a compact upright bunchgrass, usually about 40–80 cm, with threadlike involute leaves and a delicate open panicle that often develops a reddish cast. It is much smaller than Lindheimer muhly but still truly tufted, unlike creeping nimblewill.
diagnostic_traits: densely tufted perennial bunchgrass with shallow condensed rhizome
very fine filiform/involute blades about 1–2 mm wide
membranous ligule usually around 2–4 mm, sometimes longer
panicle often develops reddish to pinkish-purple cast at bloom
spikelets larger/coarser than Lindheimer muhly, with lemmas roughly 3.5–5 mm
awn usually present and can extend several millimeters

confusers.separator: Lindheimer muhly is much taller and coarser, with much longer ligules and a much larger feathery panicle.
Pink muhly can look similar at a glance but is not a project-native Central Texas taxon; use provenance plus blade/ligule/spikelet details rather than plume color.
Nimblewill has decumbent branching stems that root at lower nodes and forms low mats/patches rather than a compact basal tuft.
